entries.def: Adopted at the UN climate conference in Paris, the Agreement set a collective goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, pursuing efforts toward 1.5°C, through nationally determined emissions targets that countries set and update themselves — a structure designed to be flexible enough to secure near-universal participation, at the cost of binding enforcement.

notes.t: The US has both exited and rejoined it
notes.b: The US formally withdrew in 2020 and rejoined in 2021, illustrating how dependent the agreement's participation is on individual national politics.

notes.t: Relies entirely on voluntary, self-set targets
notes.b: Unlike the earlier Kyoto Protocol's binding targets for developed nations, Paris deliberately uses a bottom-up pledge system to maximize participation.

entries.name: Kyoto Protocol
entries.hook: The first treaty with legally binding emissions targets — but the US, the era's largest emitter, never ratified it.
entries.def: Building on the 1992 UN climate framework, the Kyoto Protocol set binding greenhouse gas reduction targets for developed nations, backed by market mechanisms like emissions trading. The US signed but never ratified it, and it was eventually superseded by the more flexible Paris Agreement structure in 2015.

left.label: Kyoto's approach
left.note: Binding targets, only for developed nations.

right.label: Paris's approach
right.note: Voluntary targets, for essentially all nations.

notes.t: The US never ratified it
notes.b: The Senate had already voted 95-0 against any climate treaty that didn't bind developing nations too, before Kyoto was even finalized.

notes.t: Introduced international emissions trading
notes.b: Its carbon market mechanisms became the template many national and regional cap-and-trade systems later drew from.

entries.name: Schengen Agreement
entries.hook: European nations agreed to remove their internal border checks entirely — creating the largest passport-free zone in the world.
entries.def: Signed by five countries on a boat on the Moselle River, the Schengen Agreement gradually eliminated passport and border controls between member states, creating a single area — now encompassing most of the EU plus several non-EU states — where people can cross internal borders without stopping for checks.

nodes.label: 5 countries sign, 1985
nodes.note: Aboard a boat on the Moselle

nodes.label: Zone expands to most of Europe

notes.t: Now covers 29 countries
notes.b: The zone has expanded well beyond its 5 original signatories to most of Europe, including several non-EU states.

notes.t: Strained by the 2015 migration crisis
notes.b: Several member states temporarily reinstated internal border checks during the European migrant crisis, testing the agreement's core premise.

entries.name: Two Plus Four Agreement
entries.hook: In one treaty, the four WWII Allied powers formally gave up their remaining rights over Germany — clearing the way for reunification.
entries.def: Negotiated by East and West Germany plus the four WWII Allied powers (US, UK, France, USSR), the Treaty ended the Allies' remaining postwar occupation rights over Germany, confirmed Germany's post-1945 borders as final, and cleared the last legal obstacle to German reunification, which followed within months.

notes.t: Confirmed Germany's postwar borders permanently
notes.b: A key Soviet condition — final confirmation that a reunified Germany wouldn't reopen territorial claims from WWII.

notes.t: Cleared reunification in under a year of the Wall falling
notes.b: The speed from the Wall's fall to formal reunification surprised even many diplomats involved at the time.

entries.name: Panama Canal Treaties
entries.hook: The US agreed to hand over one of its most strategically vital assets — the canal it had controlled for over 60 years.
entries.def: Negotiated by President Carter and Panama's Omar Torrijos, the treaties set a schedule for the US to transfer full control of the Panama Canal to Panama by the end of 1999, ending nearly a century of direct US control over the strategically critical waterway — a politically unpopular decision in the US at the time.

notes.t: Deeply controversial in the US Senate
notes.b: Ratification passed the Senate by only one vote more than the required two-thirds — a genuinely close call for a treaty of this significance.

notes.t: Panama has operated it successfully since
notes.b: Canal traffic and revenue have grown substantially under Panamanian management since the 1999 handover.

entries.name: Oslo Accords
entries.hook: Israel and the PLO recognized each other for the first time — and set a path toward Palestinian self-governance that stalled.
entries.def: Negotiated secretly in Norway, the Accords marked the first direct agreement between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization: mutual recognition, and a framework establishing limited Palestinian self-government in parts of the West Bank and Gaza, intended as a transition toward a fuller final-status agreement that was never reached.

nodes.label: Mutual recognition: Israel and the PLO

notes.t: Rabin, Peres, and Arafat shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize
notes.b: Awarded specifically for the Accords, before the peace process later stalled.

notes.t: Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated two years later
notes.b: By an Israeli opposed to the Accords — a stark marker of how contested the agreement was on both sides.

entries.name: Munich Agreement
entries.hook: Britain and France let Hitler annex part of Czechoslovakia to avoid war — buying a year of peace that historians call a catastrophic bet.
entries.def: Meeting without any Czechoslovak representative present, Britain, France, Germany, and Italy agreed to let Germany annex the Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia, in exchange for Hitler's promise to seek no further territorial expansion. Germany invaded the rest of Czechoslovakia within six months, and Poland less than a year later.

nodes.label: Germany invades the rest of Czechoslovakia within months

notes.t: 'Appeasement' became a lasting cautionary term
notes.b: This agreement is the primary historical reference point whenever the strategy of conceding to an aggressor to avoid war is invoked, almost always critically.

notes.t: Bought roughly 11 months, not lasting peace
notes.b: Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939 began WWII well within a year of the agreement.

entries.name: Brexit Referendum
entries.hook: By a margin of about 4 points, UK voters chose to leave the European Union after 43 years of membership.
entries.def: In a nationwide referendum, 51.9% of UK voters chose to leave the European Union, triggering years of negotiation over trade, borders (especially with Northern Ireland), and citizens' rights before the UK formally exited in January 2020 and left the EU's single market and customs union at the end of that year.

notes.t: The Irish border became the hardest problem
notes.b: Avoiding a hard border with EU-member Ireland while leaving the EU's customs union required a specific, still-contested Northern Ireland Protocol.

notes.t: Narrower than many expected
notes.b: Pre-referendum polling had been close, but the actual outcome still came as a significant shock to financial markets the next morning.

entries.name: Belt and Road Initiative
entries.hook: China is financing ports, railways, and highways across dozens of countries — the largest infrastructure investment program in history.
entries.def: Announced by Xi Jinping, the Belt and Road Initiative funds infrastructure — ports, railways, roads, pipelines — across Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America, deepening China's economic and diplomatic ties with participating countries while drawing criticism from some Western analysts over 'debt-trap' lending concerns.

notes.t: Sri Lanka's Hambantota Port is the most-cited case
notes.b: Sri Lanka leased the Chinese-financed port to a Chinese state firm for 99 years after struggling to repay its debt — the case most often invoked in 'debt-trap' criticism, though the framing itself remains disputed by researchers.

notes.t: The largest infrastructure program by any single country
notes.b: By total committed investment, it dwarfs earlier comparable efforts like the Marshall Plan, adjusted for scale.

entries.name: Treaty of Rome
entries.hook: Six countries agreed to form a common market — the direct founding document of what became the European Union.
entries.def: Signed by France, West Germany, Italy, and the Benelux countries, the Treaty established the European Economic Community, creating a common market with free movement of goods, services, capital, and eventually people among members — the institutional and legal foundation later treaties (including Maastricht) built the modern EU on top of.

nodes.label: Common market, free movement goals set

notes.t: Built directly on the 1951 Coal and Steel Community
notes.b: The same six countries simply expanded their existing cooperation from two industries into a full common market.

notes.t: Its 'ever closer union' phrase is still debated today
notes.b: The Treaty's founding language about deepening integration remains a live political flashpoint in debates over EU sovereignty.

entries.name: Cuban Missile Crisis Resolution
entries.hook: The world's closest brush with nuclear war ended with a secret trade neither superpower publicly admitted for decades.
entries.def: After the US discovered Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, a 13-day standoff ended with a public deal (Soviet missiles removed, US pledges not to invade Cuba) and a secret one — the US quietly agreed to remove its own missiles from Turkey — a resolution kept confidential for over 25 years to avoid the appearance of a US concession.

nodes.label: Public deal: missiles removed, no US invasion
Secret deal: US missiles leave Turkey too

notes.t: The secret Turkey trade stayed hidden for decades
notes.b: It wasn't publicly confirmed until the 1980s-90s, once key participants began writing memoirs and archives were declassified.

notes.t: Directly led to the US-Soviet 'hotline'
notes.b: The crisis's near-miss communication delays led directly to the creation of a direct emergency communication link between Washington and Moscow the following year.

entries.name: Crimea Annexation
entries.hook: Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine following a disputed referendum — a move most of the world refused to recognize.
entries.def: After Ukraine's pro-Russian president was ousted in the Euromaidan protests, Russian forces took control of Crimea, and a subsequent referendum (widely regarded by the international community as illegitimate, held under military occupation) reported overwhelming support for joining Russia. The UN General Assembly voted to declare the referendum invalid; most countries still recognize Crimea as Ukrainian territory.

nodes.label: Russian forces take control of Crimea
Russia annexes; most of the world does not recognize it

notes.t: UN General Assembly declared the referendum invalid
notes.b: A 2014 resolution affirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity, with 100 countries voting in favor.

notes.t: Directly preceded the far larger 2022 invasion
notes.b: The 2014 annexation is widely treated by analysts as the opening phase of the conflict that escalated into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

entries.name: ASEAN Founding
entries.hook: Five Southeast Asian nations, several recently at odds, agreed to cooperate economically instead — now a 10-member bloc.
entries.def: Founded by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand amid Cold War-era regional tensions, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations aimed to promote economic growth and regional stability through cooperation rather than conflict — later expanding to 10 members and becoming one of the world's most significant regional economic and diplomatic blocs.

notes.t: Founded partly to reduce regional Cold War tensions
notes.b: Several founding members had recent territorial or political disputes with each other — cooperation was explicitly meant to defuse this.

notes.t: Now a combined economy among the world's largest
notes.b: ASEAN's combined GDP today ranks among the largest economic blocs globally, alongside the EU, US, and China.

entries.name: African Union Founding
entries.hook: Africa replaced its Cold War-era unity body with one holding real authority to intervene in member states' conflicts.
entries.def: Succeeding the more limited Organisation of African Unity (founded 1963), the African Union was established with a broader mandate — including, notably, the explicit authority to intervene militarily in a member state during grave circumstances like genocide or war crimes, a power its predecessor never held.

left.label: OAU, 1963-2002
left.note: Strict non-interference in members' internal affairs.

right.label: African Union, 2002
right.note: Explicit authority to intervene in grave circumstances.

notes.t: Explicitly created power to intervene in genocide
notes.b: This was a deliberate response to the international community's failure to stop the 1994 Rwandan genocide under the OAU's old non-interference norm.

notes.t: Now 55 member states
notes.b: Covers essentially the entire African continent, making it one of the largest regional political bodies in the world.
